core: Monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes
Barriers to entry sustain monopoly: legal (patents, licenses), natural monopoly from economies of scale, control of a key resource, and network effects
The monopolist is a price maker facing the entire downward-sloping market demand curve
Marginal revenue lies below price because selling one more unit requires cutting the price on all units
The monopolist maximizes profit at the quantity where MR = MC, then charges the price the demand curve allows at that quantity, so price exceeds marginal cost
Monopoly produces a lower quantity at a higher price than a competitive market, creating deadweight loss (allocative inefficiency)
supporting: Natural monopoly and the basic idea that such firms are regulated rather than broken up
Price discrimination named as charging different buyers different prices
One-line contrast with perfect competition: P > MC under monopoly versus P = MC under perfect competition
outOfScope: Derivation of the cost curves themselves (handed to the costs topic)
Oligopoly and monopolistic competition mechanics (named only)
Antitrust law and merger policy detail
Detailed models of price discrimination (first/second/third degree)

claims.claim: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a good that has no close substitutes, sustained by barriers to entry.

Barriers to entry include legal barriers (patents lasting 20 years in the U.S., licenses, statutory monopolies such as the Postal Service's first-class mail), natural monopoly arising when economies of scale are large relative to market demand, and control of a scarce physical resource (historical examples: ALCOA and bauxite, De Beers and diamonds).

A monopoly faces the whole market's downward-sloping demand curve and is a price maker, unlike a perfectly competitive firm which is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price.

A single-price monopolist's marginal revenue is below the price because selling an additional unit both adds the price of that unit and forces a lower price on all prior units that would otherwise have sold for more.

The monopolist maximizes profit at the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then sets the highest price the demand curve permits at that quantity; because that price is read off the demand curve above marginal revenue, price is always greater than marginal cost.

Compared with a perfectly competitive market, a monopoly produces a lower quantity at a higher price; because price exceeds marginal cost, output falls short of the allocatively efficient level and society bears a deadweight loss.
Price discrimination, charging different buyers different prices for the same good, can raise the quantity sold and shrink the deadweight loss, while shifting surplus toward the seller.
Utilities that are natural monopolies (electricity, water) are commonly granted a legal monopoly and then regulated rather than split into competitors.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, 9.2 How a Profit-Maximizing Monopoly Chooses Output and Price
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the monopolist facing the whole downward-sloping market demand curve as a price maker (versus the competitive price taker), marginal revenue lying below price because raising quantity lowers the price on all previous units, the MR = MC profit-maximizing rule with price read off the demand curve, that price is always greater than marginal cost under monopoly (P = MC under perfect competition), and the resulting lower quantity at a higher price (allocative inefficiency).
